extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and practitioners advising on or drafting patent licenses
extracted.subtask_description: Legal principles governing the creation, scope, interpretation, duration, remedies, and incidental rights of licenses under patents (U.S. common-law treatise formulations). Useful for drafting, litigating, and advising about patent licensing rights and obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a license (vs assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is permission by the patentee to do acts which, without such permission, would infringe the patent; it does not amount to an assignment or to a grant of the entire and unqualified monopoly and may be granted any time after the application for patent is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of licenses only include exclusive rights limited to some but not all of make/use/sell (e.g., make & sell but not use; make & use but not sell; use & sell but not make; rights limited to certain purposes; exclusive conveyance of some but not all patent claims). The right to manufacture, sell, and use are substantive rights that can be separately granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied ancillary rights doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of express reservation, some licenses are extended by implication to convey not only what they expressly cover but also such additional rights as are necessary for the full enjoyment of the expressly conveyed right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on common-law maxim that a grant of a thing implies grant of what is necessary to make the granted thing useful to the grantee; this is a rule of legal effect of the written language, not a parol evidence enlargement of the writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express license to make specimens — implied use or sale required
rubrics_metrics.description: An express license to make specimens of a patented thing is without value unless it implies a right to use or a right to sell the specimens made thereunder; it is not to be presumed that a bare right to make only was the subject of a valuable paid license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the implied right is to use or to sell depends on surrounding circumstances — if the licensee is engaged in using the thing, imply a right to use; if engaged in making and selling for others, imply a right to sell. Do not imply both use and sell from an express license to make, because only one is necessary for beneficial enjoyment. An express license to make specimens does not imply a license to use a particular patented machine merely because that machine was the best known means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express license to use specimens implies right to make and to employ others (and to repair/replace)
rubrics_metrics.description: An express license to use a limited or unlimited number of specimens implies a right to make those specimens and to employ others to make them, and will protect those others in making them for the licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the license covers a period longer than one specimen's life, there is an implied right to repair, rebuild, or replace by making or purchasing a replacement specimen; the right to employ others for making is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express license to sell does not imply right to make (but implies downstream use/resale)
rubrics_metrics.description: An express license to sell specimens of a patented thing does not imply any right to make those specimens if they can be presumed obtainable by purchase; however, a license to sell implies that purchasers (vendees) obtain rights to use and to sell again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: no person requires a license merely to buy an article covered by a patent; a license to sell therefore typically carries implied rights for purchasers so sales are not limited to export-only assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to make & use does not authorize sales; purchasers get only conveyed rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make and use does not authorize any sale of the thing so made, nor authorize any purchaser of that thing to use it beyond the rights the seller had (express or implied). The purchaser acquires no more right to use an article useful only to produce a patented article, to be combined into a patented combination, or to perform a patented process, than the seller had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: a purchaser of apparatus from the owner of the patent acquires whatever right the patent covers to use that apparatus; purchaser may also acquire an implied license to use an owner-claimed device with similar apparatus bought from other makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to make & sell implies downstream use and resale; limits on re-use
rubrics_metrics.description: An express license to make and sell implies a right in purchasers to use and to resell the thing lawfully sold; a specimen sold with authority and without restrictions passes out of the exclusive patent right as to its unrestricted use in that condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That rule does not allow the purchaser to recombine parts with another machine to construct a new infringing device. Sales may properly be accompanied by restrictions as to methods, purposes, prices, or leasing/resell conditions, but such restrictions are not operative against a subsequent purchaser who had no notice of them at purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express licenses can be restricted to avoid implied rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Express licenses that, if unrestricted, would carry implied rights may be drafted with restrictions (territory, time, export, materials, etc.) such that the implied rights do not arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: license to make & sell restricted to particular parts of the U.S. for making and other parts for selling; restrictions may cover export, limited territory, limited time, or limiting materials operated on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair versus reconstruction limits (owner's repair rights and third-party repair suppliers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser may repair a patented machine by replacing broken or worn-out unpatented parts so long as the identity of the machine is not destroyed and the machine is not an infringement; suppliers furnishing repair parts on the order of the purchaser are not liable for infringement absent a reservation by the patentee to supply such parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right to furnish repair parts is measured by the user's right to repair. A person may improve a machine for his own use by substituting unpatented corresponding parts. But unauthorized reconstruction (rebuilding to effect an improvement rather than repair), replacement of patented parts patented to another, or reconstructing mutilated specimens by adding missing parts is unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality: written vs oral licenses and enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses may be written or oral; written licenses have advantages — can be made exclusive, proved with more certainty, and avoid statute-of-frauds problems that may render oral agreements unenforceable if non-performable within a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A written license purported exclusive will operate only as exclusive if the grantor had authority to give exclusive rights. A license is valid if made before or after patent issuance; a contract for a license can be enforceable as a license even if no formal license is subsequently executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation not required; licenses bind assignees and the world
rubrics_metrics.description: No license need be recorded, and recording does not affect the rights of any person; a license is good against the world whether recorded or not, and a purchaser or assignee of a patent takes subject to all outstanding licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license is embodied in two papers where one limits the other, an assignee of the broader instrument takes subject to the limitation in the narrower even if unrecorded and even if the assignee lacked notice. Where licenses conflict, the first in time prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses by co-owners and joint actors
rubrics_metrics.description: A license from one of several owners in common of a patent right is as good as if given by all; a license given to one of several joint makers or users is as good as if given to all if the licensor understood the licensed act was to be done jointly or by the licensee on behalf of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle applies to co-ownership and joint makers/users when the licensor's understanding contemplates the joint performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of written licenses (contract principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of a license in writing follows the same general rules as construction of other written contracts and is construed in the light of circumstances surrounding its execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: where owner of several patents licenses a person to make/use/sell a class of things that would infringe all those patents, the license confers rights under them all (even if licensor's title accrued later). Royalties are construed as payable during the lives of the patents unless language says otherwise. The grant of a 'license under said letters patent' conveys full rights to make/use/sell absent qualifying language.

rubrics_metrics.name: No implied warranty of patent validity (royalty obligations despite invalidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: No warranty of the validity of the patent is implied in any license; proof of invalidity is no defense to a suit for promised royalties — the licensee must pay royalties he promised while he enjoys the exclusive benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions/nuances: a licensee who purchases a conflicting patent may assert it against the licensor; licensee must pay royalties on what infringes the patent (acts near enough to infringe). Licensee cannot renounce license without licensor consent except in cases of licensor's false representations as to royalty rates; a license implies protection against eviction and eviction is a defense to royalties accruing after eviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eviction as discharge of royalty obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee is 'evicted' (defense to royalties thereafter) when the patent is adjudged void in an interference or in suit by the United States, or held void in an infringement suit, or when enjoined at suit of owner of a senior patent whose judgment restrains the licensee's acts under the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single successful unlicensed defiance is generally insufficient to constitute eviction; subsequent grants of licenses at lower rates by patentee do not amount to eviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied warranty of the license itself (licensor's authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: An implied warranty of the validity of the license itself appurtenant to every license given under a patent prevents the licensor from repudiating the license on the ground that he had no authority to execute it at the time; the licensor may be liable for injunction if he employs the invention covered by the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implied warranty may confer upon the licensee the benefit of any estate the licensor later acquires in the patent to the extent that benefit would have been appurtenant to the license had the estate belonged to the licensor when the license was executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration, surrender, termination, and forfeiture of licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A license not expressly limited in duration continues until the patent expires, or until surrendered pursuant to its own provisions, terminated by new agreement, or forfeited by the licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeiture does not follow merely from a single covenant breach unless parties expressly agreed forfeiture should follow; courts disfavor forfeitures and will look for waiver or agreement. Mere non-payment of a fee on due date will not necessarily work forfeiture (e.g., absence of certainty as to place of payment and lack of demand). Surrender restores parties to pre-license relations. Where license contains no forfeiture clause, owner may sue only after mutual consent termination or court decree; owner cannot prove forfeiture in an infringement suit as if deciding forfeiture in that action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner's remedies when license terminated/forfeited (infringement suit vs royalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a license is truly forfeited and the licensee continues to act, the licensor has the option to sue the licensee as an infringer or to sue for the promised royalties; suing as infringer is treated as repudiation of the license and allows the licensee to assert any defenses available absent a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: if licensee continues to mark articles as made under patent or has covenant not to contest validity, estoppel may prevent licensee's defenses for the life of the patent. If licensor sues for royalties, defendant may introduce prior art to guide construction of the patent and determine what of the licensee's acts are royalty-bearing. Choice of remedy has strategic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture may strip use of trade identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license to make and sell also conferred the right to designate those articles by an arbitrary identifying name, forfeiture of the license will disentitle the licensee to use that identifying name to designate competing articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of forfeiture can extend beyond patent rights to ancillary rights granted by the license (e.g., use of a trade name or mark tied to the licensed manufacture/sale).
